entries.clue: Aplomb – or kind of a trick? (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The second definition names the answer as the word that labels a kind of trick rather than as a trick itself; the compound does the work.

blocks.note: Self-possession, the composure of somebody who knows exactly what they are doing.
The swindle that works by first winning the victim's trust, then taking the money.

annotation.walkthrough: One word with a respectable sense and a criminal one, and the dash is all that separates them. The trick is the con artist's, sold on trust rather than sleight of hand.
annotation.definitionFit: Confidence is aplomb, poise under pressure; it also names the confidence trick, the fraud that depends on the mark's trust.

entries.clue: Prune extract (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The first definition is a verb and the second a noun; one spelling serves both readings without changing shape.

blocks.note: To cut a hedge or a beard back with shears.
A short piece lifted out of a film or a recording and shown on its own.

annotation.surface: A bottled concentrate made from dried plums.
annotation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase, 'prune extract' is something in a health-food aisle, and that reading hides the join between two separate definitions. The second is the film editor's noun.
annotation.definitionFit: To clip is to prune, cutting growth back; and a clip is an extract taken out of a longer piece of film.

entries.clue: Heavily armed and dim – peacekeepers flipping! (7)

indicatorNotes.flipping: Something flipping is turned over, so the letters it applies to come back the other way round.

blocks.note: The peacekeepers are the UN, the United Nations, and flipping turns the pair round.
Dim is UNCLEAR, so once its opening UN has been flipped the CLEAR behind it stands untouched.

annotation.surface: Soldiers both heavily armed and slow-witted, while the peacekeepers lose their tempers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping!' reads as exasperation, which is what hides the instruction. Dim supplies a seven-letter word that happens to open with the peacekeepers, so only those two letters move.
annotation.definitionFit: A state described as nuclear is armed with atomic weapons, the heaviest armament there is.

entries.clue: At home, Mark supposing that Everyman is able to take time to be petty (13)

blocks.note: Somebody at home is in.
A mark left on something is a sign of it.
If is the word that introduces a supposition.
The setter of this puzzle signs himself Everyman, so he is I.
Can is the verb for being able.
T is the standard abbreviation for time.

annotation.surface: At home with Mark, who assumes the setter has a moment to spare for small-mindedness.
annotation.walkthrough: Six pieces arrive in the order the clue gives them, which is rare over thirteen letters. Everyman is one of the few setters who names himself in his own clues, and there he is worth one letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Something insignificant is petty: too small to weigh in whatever is being decided.

entries.clue: Fright being topless, a mistake (5)

indicatorNotes.being topless: Being topless is being without a top, and the top of a down entry is the letter at its head.

blocks.note: A fright is a terror.
The letter standing at the head of TERROR, and the one that goes.

annotation.surface: A scare caught with its top off, which was a mistake.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down entry the top is the first letter, so the loss comes off the front rather than the end. Everyman keeps the cheeky sense of topless in play while doing something quite dry with it.
annotation.definitionFit: An error is a mistake — a slip in a sum, a statement or a piece of work.

entries.clue: Chair reupholstered with lamé fabric (5,4)

indicatorNotes.reupholstered: Reupholstering strips a covering off and puts the same material back in a different arrangement, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: Five of the nine letters.
The shiny metallic cloth, its accent dropped, supplies the other four.

annotation.surface: An armchair given a new covering in shimmering lamé.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fabric' sits at the end looking like part of the furniture and is the definition. Camel hair is cloth woven from the soft undercoat the animal sheds each summer.
annotation.definitionFit: Camel hair is the fabric woven from a camel's soft underwool, best known in overcoats.

entries.clue: 4, whichever way you look at it! (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a cross-reference rather than a word: 4 down is ERROR, and the answer is a colloquial term for one.
indicators: whichever way you look at it

indicatorNotes.whichever way you look at it: Looking at a word whichever way means starting from either end, which only works when the letters are arranged symmetrically.

blocks.note: The definition end: 4 down is ERROR, and this is a familiar word for making one.

blocks.clueFragment: whichever way you look at it!
blocks.note: The wordplay end: four letters reading the same from either direction, which is all the help on offer.

annotation.walkthrough: The meaning is parked in another clue and the wordplay is only a symmetry, so 4 down has to be solved first. Everyman's exclamation mark is enjoying the rude sense of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: A boob is an error, a blunder — to boob is to make one, and the noun follows from that.

entries.clue: Crossword setter’s into dictionary, mate: that’s kind of complex (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is an adjective and the definition a noun phrase: it names the kind of complex the word labels.

indicatorNotes.into: Into puts one thing inside another, so the letter it governs is dropped in among the letters around it.

blocks.note: The OED is the Oxford English Dictionary, the reference cryptics lean on.
A setter writing about himself is I.
A mate is a pal.

annotation.surface: A setter buried in the dictionary, telling a friend how complicated the job is.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'complex' at the end is Freud's, not the setter's difficulty — that switch is where the clue hides. Everyman referring to himself is worth a single I, and the dictionary is the usual three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The Oedipus complex is Freud's name for a boy's desire for his mother, and Oedipal is the adjective that labels it.

entries.clue: Where you might get a flat top – hopefully not from the tenor (10)

annotation.definition: Where you might get a flat top – hopefully not from the tenor

blocks.clueFragment: Where you might get a flat top
blocks.note: The surface offers a haircut: a flat top is the squared-off crop you ask for in the chair.
The second reading is musical: the close-harmony quartet carries a tenor, and a flat note from him would wreck the chord.

annotation.surface: Somewhere offering a flat-top haircut, with a nervous eye on the tenor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flat' does two jobs at once — the shape of the crop and a note sung under pitch — and the tenor is there to sing it. Haircuts and four-part harmony share one name.
annotation.definitionFit: A barbershop is where a flat top is cut, and a barbershop quartet is the unaccompanied four-part singing in which a flat tenor ruins everything.

entries.clue: Cutter between Channel Islands, losing direction, distressed (7)

indicatorNotes.losing direction: Losing direction asks for a compass letter to go, and one of the four is sitting in the word.

blocks.note: To be between things is to be in among them.
CI is the abbreviation for the Channel Islands, the British islands lying off the coast of Normandy.
Distressed is SORE, less the E of east.

annotation.surface: A small boat between the Channel Islands, off course and in trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: A cutter is a boat, and the surface keeps it at sea in bad weather; here it is a tooth. Of the four compass letters only east is available to lose.
annotation.definitionFit: An incisor is one of the chisel-edged front teeth, the ones that cut food off rather than grind it.

entries.clue: Bullfighter Damon shown exit, we hear (7)

indicatorNotes.we hear: We hear asks for the sound of the words rather than their spelling, so say the fragment aloud and write down what you get.

blocks.note: Damon is the film actor Matt Damon, and to be shown a door is to be shown the way out; spoken, the three words run together.

annotation.surface: Somebody called Damon being thrown out, by the sound of it.
annotation.walkthrough: The surname is there for the first name, a habit worth knowing: Damon means Matt. 'Shown exit' is the idiom shown the door with its article kept for the extra letter.
annotation.definitionFit: The matador is the bullfighter who leads the final act of a corrida and kills the bull.

entries.clue: They go up and down in tailspin, storm raging (13)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer instead of replacing it: a sentence about what these people do rather than a noun to swap in.

indicatorNotes.raging: Something raging is violently disordered, and letters caught up in it come out in another arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: Something rising and falling inside a plane's tailspin while a storm rages.
annotation.walkthrough: The two fodder words are the only concrete nouns in a sentence about weather and aircraft, which is why they read as scenery rather than letters. 'They go up and down' describes the people instead of naming them.
annotation.definitionFit: Trampolinists spend their whole sport bouncing up and down off the bed, which is all the definition claims.

entries.clue: ‘Paella?’ groaned displaced American writer (5,5,3)

indicatorNotes.displaced: Something displaced has been shifted out of its proper place, and so has every letter here.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: A diner groaning at the suggestion of a Spanish rice dish.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Paella?' look like reported speech rather than material to shuffle. Poe's full name runs to exactly the thirteen letters the two words hold.
annotation.definitionFit: Edgar Allan Poe was the American writer of Gothic tales and 'The Raven', and the first of the detective story.

entries.clue: Somewhat extrovert, he topes too much (4-3-3)

indicatorNotes.Somewhat: Somewhat means partly, so only a part of the words that follow is wanted — the part running straight through them.

blocks.note: The run starts four letters into 'extrovert' and carries on unbroken through the two words behind it, stopping two letters short of the end.

annotation.surface: A fairly outgoing man who drinks a great deal more than he should.
annotation.walkthrough: To tope is to drink habitually, an old word Everyman keeps in circulation. The hidden run straddles three words and starts four letters into the first, which is why the join stays invisible.
annotation.definitionFit: Something over the top is excessive — too much, carried past the point anyone needed.

entries.clue: Jury’s findings after court’s thrown out Italian scorer (5)

indicatorNotes.thrown out: Thrown out means got rid of, so the letters named are struck from the word they were sitting in.

blocks.note: What a jury returns are its verdicts.
CT is the standard abbreviation for court and its apostrophe-s adds the S; those three letters are the ones that go.

annotation.surface: The jury's conclusions, arrived at after the court has thrown the case out.
annotation.walkthrough: Three letters leave, not two, because the apostrophe-s goes out with the abbreviation it is attached to. 'Scorer' is the setter's word for a composer, one who writes scores.
annotation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Verdi was the Italian composer of Aida and La traviata, so he scored for a living.

entries.clue: Runners’ trainers? (9)

blocks.note: The surface offers athletes; a runner is also a climbing bean, the sort that needs something to climb.
Trainers reads as the shoes or the coaching staff; in a garden a trainer is whatever a plant is trained up.

annotation.surface: The footwear, or perhaps the coaching staff, belonging to a group of athletes.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words desert the running track for the vegetable patch, where runner beans are trained up a cane as they climb. The question mark is the only warning given.
annotation.definitionFit: Runner beans climb whatever is stood beside them, and a beanpole is the cane that does the training — the garden sense of both words at once.

entries.clue: Badly bred, dined staying in PJs? (9)

indicatorNotes.Badly: Something done badly is done wrong, and letters put together wrongly arrive in the wrong order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: Someone of poor breeding who took dinner in their pyjamas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Badly bred' holds together as a phrase, which is exactly why the first word is easy to read past as insult rather than instruction. PJs are pyjamas.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody bedridden cannot get up at all, so pyjamas stay on all day — the clue's light way of saying confined to bed.

entries.clue: Excess denim – rare – fancy! (9)

indicatorNotes.fancy: To fancy something up is to work it into a different shape, and these letters are worked into another order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A delighted cry over a heap of leftover denim, rare stuff at that.
annotation.walkthrough: Four words separated by dashes, any of which could be the definition, and the punctuation gives nothing away. 'Fancy!' reads as surprise while quietly issuing the order.
annotation.definitionFit: A remainder is what is left over once the rest has gone — the excess of a print run or of a sum.

entries.clue: Butcher’s second wife unhappy (3,4)

blocks.note: A mo is a moment, the everyday British word for a second or two.
W is the standard abbreviation for wife.
Somebody unhappy is down.

annotation.surface: A butcher's second wife, in low spirits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second wife' holds together so naturally that it hides two separate pieces, and the butcher is a verb rather than the man behind the counter. A mo is a moment.
annotation.definitionFit: To butcher a body of men is to mow them down, killing indiscriminately and in numbers.

entries.clue: Part of caterpillar going slowly (5)

indicatorNotes.Part of: Part of something is a piece taken as it stands, its letters still in the order they were given.

blocks.note: The run begins three letters from the end of the caterpillar and finishes two letters into the word behind it.

annotation.surface: A caterpillar making its way along at its own unhurried pace.
annotation.walkthrough: The hidden run needs both words, so 'going' is material rather than instruction — the temptation is to read it as the clue's verb. Largo is the marking at the slow end of a score.
annotation.definitionFit: Largo is the tempo direction telling a player to take the music slowly and broadly.

entries.clue: Basic facts; a little conflict’s arisen (3,4)

indicatorNotes.arisen: In a down entry whatever has arisen has come up the grid, so its letters are read from the bottom towards the top.

blocks.note: A conflict is a WAR, and climbing the grid it arrives this way round.
A little of something is A TAD, likewise read from the bottom up.

annotation.surface: A small quarrel that has broken out over something.
annotation.walkthrough: Turning the phrase over moves the gap between the words, so the two-word answer divides nowhere near where the clue's words do. A tad is a little.
annotation.definitionFit: Raw data is information as first collected, before anyone has processed or interpreted it.

entries.clue: Per Spooner, the time for gardening had come: no-one told me (3,3,1,2,4)

annotation.definitionNote: Both are what somebody says when caught out, the answer asking as a question what the definition states flatly.

indicatorNotes.Per Spooner: The Reverend Spooner's trademark slip was to exchange the opening sounds of two words, so that swap is what has to be undone.

blocks.clueFragment: the time for gardening had come
blocks.note: Now was I to hoe — the gardener's moment had arrived; the opening sounds of 'now' and 'hoe' then change places.

annotation.surface: Somebody protesting that nobody warned them the gardening season had started.
annotation.walkthrough: Spooner clues want the spoken phrase first: now was I to hoe. Only the opening sounds of its first and last words trade places, leaving the three words in the middle exactly as they stand.
annotation.definitionFit: 'How was I to know?' is the standard protest of somebody excusing themselves for what nobody told them.

entries.clue: Va-va-voom, or emphatically minimal speed? (5)

indicatorNotes.emphatically: Emphasis in speech comes of saying a thing twice over, so the letter it governs arrives doubled.

blocks.note: The minimum on any speedometer is zero, written as the letter O, and said twice for emphasis: zero, zero.
MPH, miles per hour, is how speed is written on a British road sign.

annotation.surface: A word for zest, offered as an alternative to barely moving at all.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole answer is a stationary car read aloud: 00 mph. Va-va-voom reached Britain through Thierry Henry's Renault adverts, so both ends of the clue are motoring.
annotation.definitionFit: Oomph is energy, zest, allure — the va-va-voom something has when it is full of life.

entries.clue: Change hearts of greedier visitors (4)

indicatorNotes.hearts of: The heart of a word is its middle, and the plural warns that more than one word is being opened up.

blocks.note: Eight letters with a clean pair at the centre: gre|ed|ier.
Eight letters again, centred on this pair: vis|it|ors.

annotation.surface: Grasping house guests having a change of heart.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words run to eight letters, so each heart is a pair rather than a single letter. 'Change of heart' is the phrase the surface leans on while the clue means it literally.
annotation.definitionFit: To edit is to change a text — cut it, correct it, reshape it before it goes out.

entries.clue: To begin with, thoroughbred turned, went at moderate pace (7)

indicatorNotes.To begin with: To begin with asks for the beginning of the word that follows, which is its opening letter and nothing more.

blocks.note: The first letter of thoroughbred, taken off the front as the clue's opening words instruct.
Food that has turned has rotted.

annotation.surface: A racehorse turning and setting off at a steady pace.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned' reads as a horse changing direction and means gone off, the way milk does. A trot is the gait between a walk and a canter, which is what makes the pace moderate.
annotation.definitionFit: A horse that trotted went at the moderate two-beat pace between walking and cantering.

entries.clue: Mix using seeds to augment relish – delicious, primarily? (7)

annotation.definition: Mix using seeds to augment relish – delicious, primarily?

indicatorNotes.primarily: Primarily asks for what comes first, so each word in the run hands over only the letter it opens with.

blocks.clueFragment: Mix using seeds to augment relish – delicious
blocks.note: Seven words in order, each giving up its initial letter.

annotation.surface: A seed-based blend recommended for making the food it is served with taste better.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word works twice over: read straight the sentence describes the condiment, and read from the front letter by letter it spells it. 'Relish' is enjoyment here, not a rival sauce.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: mustard is a paste ground from seeds, delicious, and eaten to heighten the relish of what it accompanies.

entries.clue: Confines swans (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The second definition is broader than the answer: a pen is specifically a female swan, so the clue names the bird rather than the sex.

blocks.note: Shuts livestock into an enclosure and keeps them there.
The female swan is a pen and the male a cob, a distinction swan-keepers still make.

annotation.surface: Shutting a flock of swans safely in for the night.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words and two unrelated senses: the verb for shutting animals up, and the keeper's name for the female bird. With nothing spelt out, the enumeration is all the help there is.
annotation.definitionFit: To pen animals is to confine them in an enclosure, and pens are the female swans on the water.

entries.clue: Buff and shine statue, mostly vigorously (10)

indicatorNotes.mostly: Mostly is nearly all of it, so the word ends one letter short of where it should.
indicatorNotes.vigorously: Doing a thing vigorously means shaking it about, and letters shaken about settle in a new order.

blocks.note: The first word joins the mixture whole.
STATUE stops short of its final E.

annotation.surface: Polishing a statue hard until it gleams.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Buff' is the definition and also part of the polishing picture, which is what makes it easy to leave inside the surface. A buff is a devotee — the word comes from the buff-coloured coats of volunteer firemen.
annotation.definitionFit: A buff is an enthusiast, somebody who follows a subject for the love of it.
